# Quiet Room Operation and Emergency Notes

Fictional Cedar Lantern Dance Studio. Training fixture only; no real studio policy.

## Opening the quiet room
The room lead checks lighting, clear exits, seating and the sign-in sheet before the class block begins. The room is a supervised support space, not a waiting room for visitors or a place to store performance scenery. Its soft furnishings must not block a route to the door. Staff keep the immediate environment predictable and explain any unavoidable temporary change before inviting a student inside.

The quiet room may support at most three students at one time, excluding the supervising adult. If the room is full, the teacher arranges another supervised quiet place rather than leaving a student alone in a corridor. The capacity is counted from actual occupancy, not from the number of names expected later. Siblings accompanying a participant count if they occupy the room.

## The check-in interval discrepancy
The room-operation notes require a teacher check-in after ten minutes of an ordinary quiet-room break. The current sensory planning guide allows a different interval for the same break. These notes do not declare that operations automatically outrank planning. Staff should preserve the disagreement and obtain clarification from the support coordinator. Neither interval is a medical guarantee, a punishment timer or a rule requiring a distressed student to rejoin before support is arranged.

## Evacuation drill condition
During an evacuation drill, a student using ear defenders must have a named adult within sight who can relay the evacuation cue. The student need not remove passive ear defenders merely because a drill starts. The visible adult checks the cue and follows the recorded route. This condition supplements the ordinary class permission and visible stop signal; it does not authorize an unsupervised exit or appoint another child as the safety lead.

The room lead records a student's arrival and departure times in the private quiet-room log. Use the agreed name and the responsible teacher, without a diagnosis or a narrative about behaviour. The class teacher uses the log to maintain an accurate count. The log is not displayed in the corridor and is not repurposed as a public attendance leaderboard.

## Return to the teaching room
After a quiet-room break, the student returns with the supervising adult or through a handover directly accepted by the class teacher. A message sent into a group chat is not an accepted handover. If the class has changed rooms, confirm its new location before moving. The room lead keeps responsibility until the receiving adult acknowledges the student. A participant's confidence in finding the room does not remove the recorded support arrangement.

The receiving teacher gives a brief update on the current activity and an accessible starting point. Do not replay a missed correction as criticism or require the student to make up the break immediately. Where the support plan needs review, record a private note for the coordinator rather than asking the whole class to comment. A student's return can be gradual if the agreed plan permits it.

## Equipment and environment
The room contains wipeable seating, a dimmable lamp and a small choice of plain tactile objects. Staff inspect objects for damage before use. An item brought by a student remains their property and is not passed around without permission. Cleaning follows the room checklist; scented products are not introduced during a support session because another group happened to prefer them.

A broken lamp or unexpected noise is reported to the room lead and the student is offered an alternative supported location. Staff do not promise that the room is completely silent, soundproof or clinically therapeutic. The notes provide practical room operations, not a diagnosis, prescription or treatment programme. Questions about individual medical care go through the appropriate private support route.

## A room handover example
Three students are already present when a teacher brings another participant. The room lead identifies a second supervised space and keeps the teacher involved; the extra participant does not wait alone by the stairs. Later, a drill starts and the named visible adult relays the cue to the student using ear defenders. After the drill the return is accepted directly by the class teacher and the room log is updated. The current disagreement about ten versus fifteen minutes is sent to the coordinator, rather than hidden by changing the written support plan without discussion.

## Shared use and handover
The room can be prepared by one staff member and supervised by another. The opening check and the student handover are separate actions: a clean room is not proof that an adult has accepted responsibility for a student. Before leaving, the outgoing adult states who is present and which teacher will receive each return. The incoming adult checks the log and acknowledges the handover. A door sign can tell staff that the room is occupied without identifying the students inside or disclosing why they are using it.

## Plain-language room information
A room description can say that the light is dimmable and that a supervising adult is present. It should avoid clinical promises and avoid implying that a student is guaranteed to become calm after a fixed interval. A student who needs a different support arrangement is referred to the coordinator through the agreed route. Staff report a damaged object or a blocked exit as an operational issue with a location and time. They do not leave a vague note saying the room was difficult and expect the next adult to discover the hazard.
